title: I Let My Team Fall Apart, On Purpose
author: Gaurav Jain
summary: Jain tells a first-person story of taking over a new high-profile engineering project in Singapore and deliberately declining to mediate or control the new team as it clashed. His argument is that teams must struggle before they gel and that a leader who is always the safety net prevents the team from learning to land on its feet. He ties the story to Tuckman's stages, Wiseman's Multipliers, Lencioni's trust foundation and Maslow, and offers five takeaways, including not interrupting the storming phase, being strategically invisible, and letting silence create ownership. The turning point is that team members began turning to each other instead of to him. He closes that the greatest strength of a leader is letting go, while noting the leader should step in if things become toxic.
points: Friction in a new team is a sign of people caring, and intervening too early risks compliance rather than commitment.
Leaders who always rescue teach the team dependence; the butterfly-in-the-chrysalis image argues that struggle builds the strength to fly.
Trust forms through shared hardship more than through offsites, echoing Lencioni's position that absence of trust is the base dysfunction.
Strategic invisibility means strong presence but subtle control, and the insecurity loop of jumping in to look confident makes the team lean back.
Silence forces ownership: speaking less and doing less creates the conditions for others to grow, and the leader can only create conditions, not grant self-actualization.
quotes: But I’ve learned something over the years: If you’re always the safety net, your team will never learn to land on their feet.
Teams need to struggle before they gel. Conflict is part of the process. Chaos is the path to cohesion.
If you try to help by breaking the cocoon open, the butterfly doesn’t get strong enough to fly. The resistance is what builds the wings.
Disagreements aren’t dysfunction. They’re often the signs of people caring deeply and trying to figure things out. If you intervene too early, you risk creating compliance instead of commitment.
It’s not about being absent. It’s about being strategically invisible: strong in presence, but subtle in control. Like a climbing rope: always there, only tightening when someone slips.
But great leadership isn’t about shielding people. It’s about believing in them enough to let them struggle, and letting that struggle become their teacher.
